#304. In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits

In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park’s elephant population.

Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time.

Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured.

Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country’s four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).

The reservoir had brought farming and settlers, some of whom lived inside what later became the park. When they were moved out, the land they had cleared for their crops turned into grassland that, according to de Silva, looks very much like an African savanna. With far more food than the original forest offered, the park became famous for its big elephant herds.

But the savanna was only a stage in the forest’s comeback. Without fires and clearing, invasive plants like lantana took over. “In some places, they’re like an impenetrable thicket. Not even elephants really like to go there because there’s no food for them,” de Silva said. This is a problem because elephants tend to move where the grass is. A park with less forage, the team says, stops attracting elephants from outside while, due to limited food, fewer calves reach adulthood.

Her team watched this transformation from a vehicle, driving random routes along the park’s roads about three days a week. The team identified elephants mostly by their floppy ears, which collect holes, tears, and cuts with age. “Their ears are very individually distinct, so it’s like a fingerprint,” de Silva said. Between 2007 and 2018, the team identified 443 adult and subadult females that roamed the park.

The team focused on females because males lead more solitary lives, ranging widely in search of mates. Females live in a so-called fission-fusion society. “It’s kind of similar to humans,” Madsen said. “You might have your work friends, you might have your family, and you’re not always with those same individuals at the same time, but they’re all part of your social network.” Unlike African savanna elephants, where families follow older matriarchs, Asian elephants move more independently. This may be because Asia’s rainy environment ensures that food and water are rarely far apart and usually easier to find, so following an experienced individual brings less benefit.

Madsen reconstructed the elephants’ social network for each year, measuring the strength of each relationship by how often two animals were seen together. “You can think of it as a probability that you will see those two individuals together,” she explains. An algorithm commonly used for analyzing human social networks then picked out communities—clusters of elephants with many strong ties to one another.

For the first few years of the study, these communities seemed to hold very well. But then cracks started to appear.

Around 2012, the elephants that died or left began to outnumber the newcomers. By 2018, about 69 percent of the females seen at the start of the study were gone, even though Asian elephants can live 60 years or more. Soon after the balance tipped, communities grew smaller, more numerous and more isolated from each other. “As individuals are being lost from the network, there’s nobody filling it back in,” de Silva says.

A shrinking population naturally makes for a smaller network, so the team checked whether this was just a numbers game. They looked at a population of 59 elephants seen every year of the study, which the team referred to as residents. “If it was just an artifact of the data, those core individuals should have fairly consistent relationships. But that’s not what we saw,” Madsen said. “They were changing their relationships with each other, even though they were still there.” Among these residents, the fracturing came one to three years after the decline began.

Madsen suspects some of the lost elephants were the glue holding groups together. “If you go to a city hall meeting, it’s maybe the same group of people that constantly comes in. You’re not friends with every single other person in that group, though,” she said. “There could have been some key individuals that were lost that were holding these subgroups together.”

The first ties to go were the weakest, the casual acquaintances. These weak relationships, Madsen says, could represent animals that merely tolerate each other: “Tolerance is really important in a society, especially in large animals. If they get into conflict, it could be serious.” These weak ties, researchers argue, may still be important because they can carry information between communities.

De Silva links this fracturing to the disappearing grass. “As the competition becomes more severe, your social sphere sort of shrinks,” she said. “It’s as if they’re emphasizing the quality over the quantity of the relationships.”

Before the breakup, some network statistics fluctuated from year to year, which complex systems scientists call flickering. “If you have a light bulb that’s right on the edge of dying, it might start flickering,” Madsen said. “It’s on, it’s off, it’s on, it’s off. And then suddenly it dies.” Spotted early, she argues, such signals could serve as an early warning sign. “Hopefully, park managers and conservationists can detect that and intervene before the population collapses,” Madsen said.

The challenge is that this detection requires long-term data, and we don’t have that for many populations. What worries the researchers most is that, without early detection, we may only recognize problems after it’s too late. “If you are taking the boards out of a ship and you’re not replacing them, the ship starts to take on water,” Madsen said. “There was a point of no return where there was structural damage, but you might not have noticed it until later.”

The study’s data end in 2018, but de Silva says things haven’t improved. Her team predicted a decline in the park’s elephant population in 2019, and it now appears to be happening faster than expected. “They don’t appear to be breeding very well. A lot of the calves are not surviving,” she said. Many adult females die in their 30s and 40s, and they should be living roughly twice as long.

Part of the reason they die so young is conflict with humans. Female Asian elephants have no tusks, so ivory poaching isn’t the main threat. Instead, elephants get shot when they raid crops or startle people. Occasionally, de Silva says, they also eat explosives hidden in pumpkins some locals place to get rid of wild boars. But the bigger problem, she says, is that elephants can’t survive in the protected areas alone.

More than half of Asian elephant populations live in poor-quality habitats, and the species has lost nearly two-thirds of its likely historic range. “Management really has to be about entire landscapes,” de Silva said. “Roads and infrastructure, irrigation canals—those are the things that are hurting the elephants. It’s not really a wildlife management problem.” Her team now works with farmers outside the park, testing crops elephants are less likely to damage. “Their long-term persistence really depends on people and elephants being able to share the space safely,” she said.

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714

#303. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#301. Honor Magic8 Pro vs. Magic9 Pro Max: What's been upgraded?

A 200MP main camera and 8,800mAh battery headline Honor's new flagship, though not every spec moves forward.

If you were waiting for an Honor Magic9 Pro, you can stop. Honor hasn't announced one.

Instead, Honor's 2026 lineup tops out at the Magic9 Pro Max, with the Magic9 and Magic9 Super Edition sitting below it. It's a bit messier than the typical year-over-year Pro refresh, but the new flagship does give us a pretty good idea of where Honor allocated its upgrade budget.

The major changes are obvious: a 200MP main camera, enhanced ARRI video capabilities, a 8,800mAh battery and Qualcomm's 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. Honor is a Chinese smartphone manufacturer (and yes, the Huawei tie-in does still come up), but Huawei sold the Honor business in 2020 and stated it would retain no stake or management role in the company thereafter.

While the camera bump may be shouting "more megapixels," the interesting part is where Honor put them.

The Magic8 Pro featured a 50MP 1/1.3-inch primary camera, a 200MP 1/1.4-inch telephoto camera with 3.7x optical zoom and a 50MP ultrawide camera. The Magic9 Pro Max swaps that main camera for a 200MP 1/1.28-inch sensor and retains a 200MP 1/1.4-inch telephoto camera, although Honor lists 3.5x optical zoom instead of 3.7x. Stabilization on the main and telephoto cameras also improves from Honor's CIPA 6.5 rating to CIPA 8.0.

So the dual-200MP setup is more dramatic than the generational change. The Magic8 Pro already has a 200MP telephoto. The larger upgrade is the new main sensor, which is complemented by improved stabilization and Honor's own imaging chip, the H1. And no, 200MP does not necessarily translate to higher quality photos.

Honor's real ambition lies in video. Through its ARRI partnership, the Magic9 Pro Max features LogC3 recording, ARRI Wide Gamut 3 and 10-bit capture, plus 14 preset ARRI Looks and 87 predefined color gradings. ARRI Cinema Mode tops out at 4K 60fps, giving people who color-grade footage more to work with than a cinematic filter and a dramatic name.

The phone could "introduce up-and-coming cinematographers to the ARRI brand ... [b]y giving them access to ARRI Image Science," said David Bermbach, chief product officer at ARRI. Honor leans into that creator angle with an optional Photography Master Kit containing 200mm- and 500mm-equivalent teleconverters, an imaging grip and other accessories.

That's more than putting another camera company's logo on the back. Oppo and Vivo are already pushing 200MP sensors, teleconverters and increasingly elaborate imaging systems on their own flagships, so Honor needs something besides a megapixel arms race to stand out.

For comparison, the Magic8 Pro is equipped with a 7,200mAh battery, 120W wired charging and 80W wireless charging, based on the Chinese specifications (Honor varies battery specs by market). That's raised to 8,800mAh, or about 22 percent more capacity, with the Magic9 Pro Max, but wired charging is limited to 100W. Wireless charging is still 80W, and the wireless charger is sold separately.

The battery also carries some luggage. The Magic9 Pro Max is slightly heavier than the Magic8 Pro at 233 grams, and the display is slightly larger at 6.8 inches compared to 6.71 inches. It also introduces MagicOS 11, built on Android 17, with file transfers across supported iPhones, Macs, Android devices and Windows PCs. Honor Connect is required for iOS, macOS and Windows transfers.

Honor has not confirmed if the international variants will be equipped with the 8,800mAh battery. That 8,800mAh figure shouldn't be assumed for other markets, as the Magic8 Pro in the United Kingdom has a 6,270mAh battery, while China's version has a 7,200mAh battery.

The company hasn't even confirmed a US release, so anyone who's considered importing it would have to check network-band support, warranty coverage and regional software differences rather than assume it will act like a locally bought Galaxy or Pixel. The Magic9 Pro Max starts at 6,499 yuan in China (the equivalent of about $974).

#298. How to get better results from Google Gemini

These tips and tricks will help you prompt Gemini better.

Finding the right AI search engine can be tricky. Google's most prominent AI tool is Gemini, an AI assistant designed to deliver informative, concise answers while helping with daily workflows. It's not the most feature-rich chatbot, yet its integration with Google's own apps and ecosystems makes it a strong competitor to Claude and ChatGPT. It's an powerful tool when used properly, and making it work well starts with optimizing Gemini.

Google Gemini offers a convenient way to answer basic search questions and research a range of topics, and it can be a particularly useful companion to Google's search engine and products. That starts with integrating Gemini with your apps. You can connect your most-used apps to Gemini directly under the customization menu in the Gemini menu. We highly recommend doing this to let Gemini streamline any workflows you have.

Prompts are the cornerstone of optimizing any AI assistant, and Google Gemini is no exception. Standard prompt advice applies here: prompts with specific, detailed instructions and added context will perform much better than generic ones. Remember that AI is malleable, including its personality and the way it delivers information. To prompt with Gemini effectively, specify its role in the conversation. Is it a close friend, a mentor or a professional in a given industry? If you struggle to come up with ideas, set restrictions. Limiting sources and presentation methods is a great way to quickly tailor Gemini to your needs.

You can also shape Gemini's responses through skills, prompts that can be saved and run with a simple slash command. You can find skills listed in the customization menu. Google offers a few premade skills by default, but you can create your own and execute them as you see fit. We recommend creating a skill for different roles you need Gemini to fulfill. Once you're done, you can simply type the command to tailor Gemini without having to swap tabs.

Gemini's responses have a few chat parameters you can use. When starting a chat with Gemini, you can click the plus icon near the chat bar to display various settings. The first few options allow you to upload documents or images, but the more impactful options are at the bottom: deep research and guided learning. Deep research tailors Gemini to act as an authority in the space, requiring it to find multiple sources on a given topic before responding. This can be a great way to get detailed responses about niche topics you'd struggle to search elsewhere. Guided learning is tailored as a study guide for those learning a new subject.

Since AI algorithms are constantly evolving, Gemini likely isn't the only chatbot you're using. Google is well aware of this and allows you to import chat history from other AI chatbots to Gemini. Export your chat data from your other chatbots, then enter the settings menu for Gemini to import that data. This will help tailor Gemini's output and give it a starting memory to draw from.

#297. FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace

Airlines praised the AI tool, but the air traffic controllers’ union wasn’t involved.

The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.

“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.

However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system “cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft,” the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.

The previous FAA announcement included supportive statements from Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom.

But the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, also told Flying magazine that it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”

Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system’s coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News.

The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

Ars has previously covered the SMART system’s development and lingering questions about how it works, as well as the air traffic controller shortage and other challenges facing the FAA.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#294. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#293. This underrated Google Health app feature can make food tracking less annoying

Get a handle on how your diet is affecting your overall health.

For those keeping a close eye on their health goals, the Google Health app pairs seamlessly with Fitbit trackers and Google Pixel smartwatches. The Google Health Premium subscription tier offers many upgrades to really hone in on daily intake and activity goals, such as food and hydration tracking.

It's not necessarily a unique feature. Many fitness tracker companion apps offer nutrition logging, including Oura and Garmin. There are also popular third-party apps like MyFitnessPal that have food logging capabilities. But Google Health Premium's version is incredibly intuitive, versatile and will actually make you more inclined to use it.

We live in a day and age where everything is all about protein. Are you getting enough protein? Does this yogurt, bread or bar have sufficient protein to help you meet your daily goals? Not only that, but we're also counting carbs, calories and fat, and trying to calculate whether we're eating in a deficit and meeting or exceeding goals. This sorely underrated feature of the Google Health app is one of the best upgrades with Google Health Premium that you probably aren't using yet.

Once you sign up for Google Health Premium, available at $9.99 per month or at no extra charge through a Google One subscription, it unlocks a Nutrition section under the Health tab of the app. Here, you can see data like your calorie target (based on gender, age, height, weight, and average activity) and caloric burn and intake. It knows how many calories you burned based on steps, activity, and heart rate logged from a companion tracker or smartwatch. But how does it know how much you consumed? That's up to you to log.

There are several ways you can log a meal. Tap the "+" sign at the top right of the Nutrition card, tap the "+ Log" button under your daily summary on the Today tab, or select Food & Drink if it's within those customizable tabs. You can also select the Ask Coach assistant and type or speak details of the meal.

It's incredibly simple. Describe the meal (say "I had a coffee, banana, and coconut yogurt") or use a barcode scanner on each ingredient. The most convenient option? Just take a photo. Use that photo you were going to upload to social media anyway and upload it to the app. Alternatively, you can take one right from the app. It intelligently analyzes and identifies the dish, then calculates data from the ingredients. You can even snap a photo of a packaged item, like a box of cereal or protein bar, and watch it calculate the nutritional content accordingly.

If necessary, you can modify details as needed. Maybe you want to clarify that your Caesar salad has light dressing, for example, or that you only ate half a portion.

Logging is great, but what can you do with all this information? The more you log, the more helpful the data is. Working alongside a tracker like the Fitbit Air or Fitbit Edge, it can determine patterns. It may determine that you don't sleep well when you have caffeine or a heavy meal late at night. Perhaps you have more energy in workouts with a bigger breakfast. It can also provide recommendations on what to eat to stay within your caloric recommendations or meet your protein goals.

In the summary page for each day, you'll see an ongoing calculation of how many calories you have left to consume to either reach your target or remain in a caloric deficit in relation to how many calories you have burned. You'll also see macro goals, calculated from the meals you have logged. This includes carbs, fat, and protein. It advises where you should be for each and what percentage of that you're at.

Like any food logging app, it takes diligence to remember to add everything you consume, from your morning coffee to your afternoon snack or the cup of popcorn you snuck in at night. But it's so easy to do this by snapping photos or speaking to Ask Coach. You could sit down at night and dictate your entire day's worth of meals so it's all logged at once (and check if there's space in your calorie goals for that evening glass of wine). It's so easy to do on the fly, and one of the most underrated Google Health Premium features you should be using.

#292. EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.

"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.

But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.

Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.

"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.

European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.

Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."

This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.

"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."

Zelensky said he found the US approach "a bit strange."

Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.

The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.

Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.

Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.

But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

#290. Why your SD card won't let you transfer files bigger than 4GB, and how to fix it

Your SD card's file system might be stopping you from transferring large files, but there's an easy fix for that.

SD card capacities have grown by leaps and bounds since hitting the market in the early 2000s, and the best microSD cards now come in capacities from 128GB up to a massive 1TB. No matter how capacious your SD card, though, you may run into an unexpected limitation: it won't accept files larger than 4GB, even when there's enough space left.

While it may seem worrying, the good news is that the SD card itself is almost certainly fine. Instead, the problem lies in the file format it's currently using. More specifically, it's FAT32, a file system that dates back to Windows 95 and is still commonly used today. Although it's widely compatible and can be read by almost any device, it has a major downside: no single file can be larger than 4GB.

FAT32's 4GB-per-file limit comes down to how it records file sizes using a 32-bit number. In computing, the largest value that fits within this limit is 4,294,967,295 bytes, or nearly 4GB. The SD card can physically hold files over 4GB, but the file system prevents it. That's usually fine if you only store documents and photos, but it can quickly become a problem if you want to store 4K videos, for example. In that case, you'll need to reformat your microSD card to exFAT, another file system designed to overcome FAT32's limitations — including support for files larger than 4GB.

First, back up all the files on your SD card, since this process will erase everything. Also, if you're using very old tech (like a camera that's more than a decade old), it may not support exFAT. Microsoft added exFAT support in Windows Vista SP1, while Apple added it with OS X Snow Leopard. If your device predates either OS, it's probably best to keep your SD card formatted as FAT32.

On Windows, open File Explorer to format your SD card. Click This PC, then right-click on your SD card. Select Format from the menu that appears and choose exFAT under File System. Here, you can also choose whether to run a Quick Format or rename the volume. The process is the same as formatting a microSD card or a USB drive. On a Mac, use the Disk Utility app instead (you can quickly find it using Spotlight). With the app open, go to the View menu and click Show All Devices. Select your SD card — not the volume listed under it — then click Erase. Set the format to exFAT, name the volume and confirm.

After formatting the SD card, you can freely copy files larger than 4GB to it. If you want to switch back to FAT32, repeat the steps above and change the file system again. Keep in mind that Windows won't let you select FAT32 for cards larger than 32GB, and you'll need to use Terminal or third-party software for that.

#289. Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed

Cost and access barriers are pushing people to modified use and unapproved versions.

GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That’s around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.

Modified use of GLP-1 medications was particularly common among those using compounded versions of GLP-1 medications. Among all GLP-1 users, at least 23 percent used a compounded version; an additional 9 percent said they didn’t know whether their GLP-1 was compounded or not.

These versions of GLP-1 drugs are made by compounding pharmacies and are intended to mimic a medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration, such as Wegovy or Ozempic. But compounded drugs themselves are not approved by the FDA; the regulatory agency does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they’re sold. While compounded drugs are considered more accessible and affordable, they generally have higher rates of preparation errors, contamination, and other manufacturing problems compared to non-compounded drugs.

Among people who used these unapproved, potentially riskier GLP-1s, 62 percent were not taking them as prescribed. That’s compared to just 36 percent of GLP-1 users who took brand-name drugs.

The potential risks of taking unapproved GLP-1 drugs at all or taking them in unapproved ways may be missed by users, the CDC researchers note. A 2025 study assessing websites selling compounded GLP-1 medications found that nearly 40 percent of sites stated or implied the drugs were FDA-approved, making it harder for consumers to differentiate the compounded versions from FDA-approved ones. Further, nearly 80 percent of sites used brand names in their advertising, which could further mislead consumers. The researchers noted that using brand names violated FDA regulatory standards.

“Given the substantial use of compounded GLP-1 medications, understanding the safety and quality of compounded GLP-1 medications is an important public health consideration,” the authors conclude. They also call for more research on the common modifications people are using, such as dose and frequency adjustments, saying the data on the safety and effectiveness of these real-world practices “could help guide the development and implementation of clinical guidelines and support appropriate medication use.”

#286. One cable mistake could be killing your desktop PC's gaming performance

Your monitor might be connected to the motherboard instead of your graphics card, and the fix takes only a cable swap.

You may have a great graphics card in your gaming desktop and still be disappointed with its performance because of where the monitor is plugged in. Many PCs have HDMI, DisplayPort and USB-C monitor connections in two places: on the motherboard and on the dedicated graphics card. The same cable can fit either set of ports, which isn't particularly helpful.

If your desktop has a dedicated graphics card, the monitor should normally connect to that card's outputs. You may end up with less capable integrated graphics or a blank screen if you use a motherboard port. Instead of assuming that the problem is your hardware, start by inspecting the back of the case. The motherboard's video outputs typically use the graphics integrated into the CPU (if it has any), instead of the dedicated graphics card in a PCIe slot.

Integrated graphics are suitable for basic tasks and less demanding games, but typically cannot compete with your dedicated graphics card — even if you know how to boost GPU performance without buying new hardware. If Windows runs your game on integrated graphics instead, you're missing out on the performance of your dedicated GPU.

Plugging into the motherboard doesn't always leave the dedicated GPU idle. In some Windows configurations, that card can still render games and pass the frames through integrated graphics, potentially adding overhead. Microsoft doesn't state a percentage of performance loss for this configuration, and the impact will depend on the hardware. That's why some gamers don't notice the mistake immediately.

For others, it's a black screen. Motherboard video outputs won't work with Intel desktop processors carrying an F or KF suffix, since those chips lack integrated graphics. Some PCs also disable the integrated GPU when a dedicated card is installed, so a blank screen doesn't necessarily mean your graphics card has failed.

Luckily, the correct ports are typically easy to find. The motherboard's video outputs are grouped with its USB, Ethernet and audio ports. The graphics card has its own outputs on a separate expansion bracket, typically lower down on the back of a conventional tower. They're often horizontal rather than vertical, but orientation isn't universal, so check which ports belong to the graphics card.

Turn off the PC, move the monitor cable to the graphics card and select the corresponding input on the monitor. Both HDMI and DisplayPort support high-refresh-rate gaming, provided your graphics card, monitor and cable support the resolution and refresh rate you want. DisplayPort comes standard on most modern gaming monitors, but if you are already using HDMI and it is working at the resolution and refresh rate you need, then you don't need to purchase a new cable. For Windows 11, go to Settings > System > Display > Advanced display and check the refresh rate.

Do remember, though, that a 100Hz monitor that's set to 60Hz will only show 60 updates per second, no matter what the graphics card renders. If your screen goes black after switching to the graphics card, try a different GPU port or cable. Before checking the power connectors or seating on the card, shut down and unplug the PC. Finally, if integrated graphics aren't disabled, you can even connect a second monitor to the motherboard's output, depending on your system's compatibility.

#285. FAA has lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy blamed obsolete equipment for the outage.

The Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening. Domestic flights were cleared to begin taking off at 8:35 pm EST. FAA Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cautioned that, barring massive system updates, there will be “more of these” ahead.

“Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Duffy posted on X.

Over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday. “Due to the ongoing ground stop, Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening,” the airline said.

The stoppage began at 3:36 pm EST Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool, when the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X, citing a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff was troubleshooting the problem.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”

Mullin had said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.

This was only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13. Flights were also grounded for less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after its Notice to Air Missions system suffered an outage.

Unfortunately for travelers, it turned out to be a lengthy ground stop. Airlines were quick to cancel flights scheduled to leave later in the day, with American Airlines warning that disruptions were expected for the rest of the day.

“This is going to take some time,” Mullin said. “Flights are accounted for, and there should be no fear to the public at all.”

This story was updated at 10:03 pm EST to report the ground stop was lifted.

#283. Common reasons your Roku TV can turn on by itself and how to fix it

Some people have been experiencing random power-ons recently.

You're sound asleep in the middle of the night when, all of a sudden, your TV turns on. You know you turned off the TV before you went to bed, no one else is awake, and there's nothing near your remote to accidentally push the power button. What — or who — could have turned on the TV? A bored spirit haunting your home? A burglar looking to take a quick break?

Those scenarios are highly unlikely. But, unfortunately, some Roku TVs and Roku streaming device owners have been jolted out of their slumber by those products inexplicably powering on randomly over the past few months. And no one really knows why it's happening. There may be a few explanations, however, and a couple of potential fixes to try if your Roku device has gone rogue during the wee hours.

When Roku OS version 15.3 went live in August 2026, owners of Roku TVs and Roku streaming devices began reporting these middle-of-the-night disturbances. Not every Roku TV or streaming player has been impacted by this supposed 15.3 bug, but the timing of the reports with the software update seems more than coincidental.

What's odd about that, though, is that there was nothing in the 15.3 update that involved autoplay features or even power management. So, in theory, the changes that were made to the Roku OS shouldn't have spurred these instances of people's Roku TVs "waking up" without being powered on by anyone (or anything) and playing a TV show or movie. But we all know that software updates often introduce bugs with no real rhyme or reason, and that feels like the most logical explanation for these strange occurrences.

Having your Roku TV's HDMI-CEC feature enabled is another very plausible reason the TV powers on randomly. If you're not familiar with HDMI-CEC, it's basically a chain that links all your A/V components with built-in HDMI switching (like soundbars, gaming consoles, receivers and speakers) since they're all connected via HDMI cables. And this allows all of those devices to be controlled with one remote.

So, when you power on your Roku TV, for example, HDMI-CEC essentially notifies all the other connected components to turn on. All it takes is one glitchy signal to confuse the whole chain, which could lead to a random power-up. And there is a history of HDMI-CEC causing strange switching between inputs and components, as well as phantom power-ons. Samsung Anynet+, Sony BRAVIA Sync, LG SimpLink and Roku 1-Touch Play are all just different names for the same HDMI-CEC standard, but each has its own custom software added to it to create the proprietary HDMI-CEC feature for each brand of smart TV.

Unfortunately, compatibility sometimes becomes an issue unless all of your connected devices are made by the same company (though even that doesn't guarantee incident-free performance). This can cause signal miscommunication that results in the random behavior of your Roku TV or streaming device.

There are other possible explanations for your Roku TV turning on by itself. For example, the Fast TV Start feature is a proprietary power-management setting that keeps your Roku TV's OS on in the background even when you shut off the TV.

This allows the TV to turn on instantly without any boot time, and it keeps the TV on alert for voice commands to turn the TV back on. Fast TV Start has also seemingly caused phantom power-on problems in conjunction with the Roku OS 15.3 update, as the always-on network connection kept open the door for overnight glitches.

You may try all of these suggestions and still not have much luck because the root of the issue has not been "officially" identified by Roku, or anyone else, for that matter. And without the root cause, there remains no guaranteed fix. But these possible solutions are certainly worth trying and just might do the trick.

The first thing to try, if you haven't already, is updating your Roku TV's OS to version 16, which was released in October. Fixing the 15.3 bug wasn't part of the update, and no reports have surfaced that OS 16 patched the automatic power-on problem, but it's definitely worth trying. The worst-case scenario is that your Roku TV's OS is fully updated.

Next, disable 1-Touch Play (HDMI-CEC) not just on your Roku TV but on all the other components connected to the TV, regardless of brand. This includes your A/V equipment and gaming consoles. To do so on your Roku TV, go to Settings > System > Control other devices and uncheck 1-Touch Play. Also disable Fast TV Start, which you can find under Settings > System > Power > Fast TV Start, then either clear the Enable Fast TV Start option or check Off to disable it.

If these don't work, try unplugging the TV when you're done watching it each night (no, not ideal), using a smart plug to automatically cut the power for you or consulting Roku's tech support portal at support.roku.com for further assistance.

#282. Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday

One way or another, the company will get some more data on Saturday.

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified issue, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.

The primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.

This means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the company now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.

In that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The company has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

However, SpaceX still has a chance to make history on Saturday with the potential return of the Starship upper stage. SpaceX has never attempted to catch the vehicle’s upper stage.

Doing so will require Starship to pass a series of tests in orbit and subsequently during its return to Earth to ensure it is fully healthy. This is critical because Starship will be passing over parts of Mexico and the United States before returning to Starbase, and SpaceX does not want to endanger people on the ground. Additionally, it does not want to risk damage to its launch towers.

If Starship passes these health checks, it would land at about 3:15 pm local time in Texas (21:15 UTC). If it does not, the company has earlier options to de-orbit the vehicle into an ocean.

Successfully returning Starship’s upper stage would be historic, as well as significant for SpaceX’s efforts to reuse the massive rocket. It would also give the company valuable information about the vehicle’s performance during reentry.

One of the biggest hurdles left in Starship’s development is the vehicle’s heat shield, which must protect the upper stage during its return through Earth’s atmosphere. More than that, SpaceX aims to make Starship rapidly reusable, and to do this, Starship’s tiles must be light and resilient.

SpaceX has been experimenting with tiles since the beginning of the Starship program, trying to find the right combination of low mass, heat resistance, and durability so the tiles require minimal refurbishment between launches. For this flight, SpaceX said it is applying learnings from the previous test flight in September, including additional retention mechanisms on tiles in areas deemed to be at the highest risk of falling off during ascent and addressing areas with a flow path for plasma to get behind the tiles.

Another problem on recent flights has been heat incursion into the small gaps between the edges of the tiles. According to SpaceX, this Starship has a large portion of the heat shield equipped with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles.

#280. There's a hidden way you can check which services are running on your Android phone

Just like a desktop PC, your Android phone has a built-in task manager. Here is how to find it, monitor your memory and safely limit background apps.

If you use a desktop PC, you may be familiar with the task manager, which lets you view all the processes running in the background of your computer and taking up resources. What you may not know is that Android phones (even budget models) have the same feature, but it's kept hidden away from users, requiring a little digging to find it. If you want to keep an eye on what's using your phone's memory, it can be worth uncovering this hidden display, but you should proceed with caution before you start closing processes willy-nilly.

To check what processes are running, you first need to activate developer mode to make your phone faster. Under the Settings menu, scroll down to the bottom, tap About Phone and look for the Build number. If it's not there, you may have to enter an additional Software information menu, depending on your phone's model and Android version. Once you find it, keep tapping the Build number option until you get a message that developer mode has turned on or a dialog box asking you to confirm. Then, back out to the main Settings menu. You'll find Developer options on this main screen, or under a System submenu. Tap the option, then open Running Services. You can also select the three dots in the top right of the screen to select Show cached processes and see what's been recently suspended but still held in memory.

This is Android's version of the task manager, showing you all the running services currently providing frameworks for the apps on your phone, along with how much memory they're using. But don't start closing processes to free up that precious memory. While the task manager on PC often shows plenty of bloat that you can safely close, that's not usually the case for Android phones. The processes you see here are more likely managing features like Bluetooth, your keyboard and location settings. Shutting these down can seriously hamper your phone.

Both the Running Services and Memory menus are more like diagnostic tools. If you're having problems with your phone, it can be helpful to check here and see if anything seems wildly out of order, like a single process hogging the majority of your phone's memory. You may want to stop the related process until you can fix the underlying issue, but be prepared to restart your phone if anything goes wrong.

A better way of controlling background processes is by limiting their use. In the Developer options menu, under the Apps heading, you'll find Background process limit. This lets you limit the number of apps allowed to run in the background at one time. This default setting triggers an automatic limit based on how much RAM your phone has, which is a crucial factor in making older Android phones last longer. However, you can also change the limit to between one and four to free up memory.

Keep in mind that this will make multitasking harder and will cause a bigger performance hit at the moment you re-open apps, since your phone will have to fully restart them now.

You can also limit how individual apps behave in the background. In the Settings menu, head to Apps, select a specific app and tap Battery. The default Optimized option automatically adjusts the app's background permissions based on how you use it, but switching to Restricted limits its activity when suspended.

#279. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#277. Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business

Healthy soils, native plants, and fewer chemicals are helping vineyards adapt.

More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine, but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.

Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.

As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.

We are a team of geographers and sustainability scientists who study environmental change, environmental health, conservation, agriculture and land management. Our team wanted to better understand how farmers in South Africa’s wine-producing regions are responding as a range of environmental and economic pressures rise. We talked with growers, conservation practitioners and wine industry experts in the Western Cape and analyzed how 107 vineyards, about 20% of the total, were using sustainable land stewardship practices to adapt.

In many agricultural landscapes, production and conservation goals are frequently viewed as competing priorities. But our research found that many vineyard operators in the Western Cape see long-term stewardship and conservation of soil and wildlife habitat as essential strategies for business success.

The Western Cape is home to the Cape Floral Region, a global biodiversity hot spot. It includes fynbos, a unique biome containing thousands of endemic plant species, including types of proteas, ericas and restios that are found nowhere else on Earth.

Sustainability certification and conservation programs, such as World Wildlife Fund Conservation Champions, have helped encourage vineyards to protect biodiversity in the region. Many growers use these sustainability certifications to increase their wine’s marketability. But we found they have also embraced conservation for how it can benefit their vineyards. Rather than viewing conservation as land taken out of production, many said they see it supporting the ecological processes essential to their business.

The majority of South Africa’s vineyards today participate in the Integrated Production of Wine certification system, created by the South African wine industry and researchers in 1998 to reduce environmental harm. The system sets standards governing pesticide use, water management, wastewater treatment and environmental stewardship. It also uses independent auditing of participating farms and wineries to ensure those claiming certification meet the standards.

To manage the water supplies their vineyards depend on, growers described restoring native vegetation, including the removal of alien species, along waterways and reducing erosion to protect wetlands and rivers. Research shows that healthy natural systems can improve water retention in the soil and contribute to the overall resilience of the landscape in the face of more extreme climate conditions.

To boost their soil’s health, some growers are planting cover crops, such as legumes, cereals like oats and rye, and brassicas such as radish and mustard, between vine rows. Growers broadly described using cover crops, compost, mulching and other practices to improve soil structure and increase organic matter in the soil. Cover crops require maintenance and can provide habitat for pests, but research shows that the right cover crops, when well maintained, can benefit vineyards by reducing erosion and increasing water retention and nutrients in the soil.

Several producers also described efforts to reduce their reliance on chemical pesticides, which is beneficial not only for the environment but also their businesses as chemical costs continue to rise. We heard about vineyards that monitor pest populations closely and respond in targeted ways rather than using pesticides broadly.

Some growers encourage beneficial insects and manage habitats that support natural pest control. The creation of habitats for natural pest predators can reduce the overall disease risk too. While chemical treatments remain part of many vineyard operations, growers reported increasing interest in other approaches that prevent disease and pest outbreaks, such as pruning, to reduce their total chemical use.

Sustainable practices like these are well established in South Africa’s wine industry, but our interviews suggest their use has been expanding in recent years. Rather than focusing solely on treating problems after they arise, these approaches emphasize prevention, monitoring and ecological balance.

The stewardship practices we observed in South Africa are investments in long-term business resilience for many growers.

Many of the wine producers we interviewed described facing rising costs and market uncertainty. Exports, labor and chemicals are all expensive. They emphasized that maintaining healthy soils, conserving water and reducing vulnerability to drought and disease are essential to keeping their vineyards productive.

As concerns about drought, climate pressures and profitability rise, the area in vineyard production in South Africa has also decreased. Several growers described diversifying their business models and even switching crops to make their businesses more resilient to hotter, drier conditions.

Farmers around the world are confronting the realities of a changing climate. Our research shows that effective solutions can come from recognizing the interconnectedness of nature and production.

The experience of South Africa’s winegrowers shows that farms can be managed more sustainably when they’re seen as part of larger ecological systems.

Students Zoe Van der Walt, Jack Spining and Dryver Finch contributed to this article.

Hannah V. Herrero is Associate Professor of Geography & Sustainability and Director of Sustainability at University of Tennessee; Erin L. Bunting is Assistant Professor of Geography at Michigan State University; Jane Southworth is Professor of Geography at University of Florida; Jason K. Blackburn is Professor of Geography at University of Florida; and Stephanie Insalaco-Wyner is Assistant Professor of Geographic Information Sciences at Southwestern University.
